title: City Infrastructure Planning
short_description: Learn how city planners connect roads, utilities, stations, and public facilities while minimizing construction cost and improving accessibility using Graph BFS, Graph DFS, Dijkstra's Algorithm, Kruskal's Algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall.

real_world_context.problem: A city planner needs to design infrastructure that connects roads, utilities, stations, and public facilities across a growing city. Engineers must trace which areas can be reached from key hubs, find the most cost-effective routes between facilities, decide which connections to build at minimum cost, precompute travel times between all pairs of locations, and find efficient paths using heuristic guidance.
real_world_context.why_it_matters: Graph algorithms help city planners design efficient infrastructure networks that minimize construction costs while ensuring all areas are accessible. These algorithms are essential for urban development, emergency response planning, and transportation system design.

learning_objectives: Represent a city infrastructure network as a graph using an adjacency list.
Traverse a network with Breadth-First Search (BFS) to map all reachable facilities from a central hub.
Traverse a network with Depth-First Search (DFS) to explore connectivity and discover deep routes.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the minimum-cost route between two facilities.
Use Kruskal's algorithm to build a minimum-cost infrastructure network connecting all facilities.
Use Floyd-Warshall to precompute the shortest route between every pair of locations.
prerequisites: Introduction to graphs and adjacency lists
completion_message: You have completed the City Infrastructure Planning mission. You have learned how graph traversals, shortest-path algorithms, minimum-spanning-tree algorithms, all-pairs shortest paths, and heuristic-guided search can be used to design cost-effective and accessible city infrastructure.
